title: Attaining Rebirth in Freedom
author: Zhanran
excerpt: (The original text is taken from the Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)

inline.s: The original text is taken from the Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu
The key to attaining rebirth in freedom:
Thought after thought without interruption, until the end of life;
steeling the mind, restraining oneself, never ceasing by day or night.
When thought follows thought without interruption, the body of the sense-organs and the world are transformed thought by thought.

[Thought after thought without interruption] The thought of Buddha-recitation continues without intermingling with other thoughts. [Steeling the mind, restraining oneself] rousing oneself and disciplining oneself. [Never ceasing by day or night] by day and by night, never letting the uninterrupted succession of thoughts stop. This is diligent cultivation of the pure karma. When the pure karma is brought to completion, one will know beforehand the hour of death and attain rebirth in freedom.

[The Lankāvatāra Sutra says: “What all the sages know, handed down from one to another as their teaching, is that deluded thoughts have no nature.” The Second Patriarch said: “Seek the mind, and it is utterly unobtainable.” The Awakening of Faith says: “If there is one who can contemplate no-thought, that is turning toward the Buddha’s wisdom.” The Huayan Helun (Combined Commentary on the Flower Ornament Sutra) says: “To awaken suddenly to the single thought as dependently arisen and unborn transcends the views of the three vehicles and their provisional teachings.”]

The Lankāvatāra Sutra says: This is what the Buddhas of the past knew, now handed down one to another as their teaching: deluded thoughts have no entity — they are illusory appearances. The Second Patriarch of Chan, Huike, said: I seek the mind, and I simply cannot find it. The Awakening of Faith says: If there is one who can contemplate no-thought, that is turning toward the Buddha’s wisdom. The Huayan Helun says: To awaken suddenly to the fact that “a single thought is a dependently arisen, never-born illusion” already surpasses the views of those who follow the three vehicles and their provisional teachings.

[No nature] “Nature” means essence; all dharmas have no entity and are illusory appearances, which is called having no nature. The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are ever without nature.” The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “All illusions become without nature.” [Seek the mind, and it is utterly unobtainable] Bodhidharma said: What, after all, have you come here to seek? Huike (the Second Patriarch of Chan) replied: “My mind is not at peace; I beg you to pacify it.” Bodhidharma said: “Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it for you.” He replied: “Seek the mind, and it is utterly unobtainable.” Bodhidharma said: “I have finished pacifying your mind for you.” [Three vehicles] the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. [Provisional teachings] expedient teachings.

[These words of the sutras and the patriarchs, and the treatises composed by the bodhisattvas and great teachers, all point directly at the single thought before the mind, to reveal that the nature of the false is fundamentally empty. Now, since the false is fundamentally empty and the true is fundamentally existent, what is this if not Buddha? But sentient beings have long followed defiling conditions and have not been able suddenly to restore their fundamental emptiness. One must begin from pure conditions and gradually turn them around. With the causal mind — which is myself as Buddha — I recite the resultant Buddha — who is the Buddha of my own mind. Cause and result have always interpenetrated; mind and Buddha are naturally
(by nature)

one and the same. And the resultant Buddha of my own mind, with his unconditional great compassion and his great sympathy of one essence with all beings, is in himself inconceivable. Moreover, the causal mind — which is myself as Buddha — with its deep faith and earnest vow and its single-minded, devoted recitation of the name, is also inconceivable. If within thought after thought one can wholly settle the many defilements, perfectly reveal the fundamental emptiness, suddenly join the spiritual source, and go straight to the ocean of the fruit — well then
(in that case)
no pure condition surpasses this.]

These words of the sutras and the patriarchs, and the treatises composed by the bodhisattvas and great teachers, all point directly at the single thought before the mind, to make clear that the thought is false and its nature is fundamentally empty. Since the false is fundamentally empty and the true is fundamentally existent, is this not Buddha? It is only that sentient beings have long followed defiling conditions and have not been able suddenly to restore their fundamental emptiness. One must begin from pure conditions and gradually turn them around, so as to restore the fundamental emptiness. With the causal mind — which is myself as Buddha from the first — I recite the resultant Buddha of my own mind (Amitābha Buddha). Cause and result have always interpenetrated; mind and Buddha are naturally equal and non-dual. And the resultant Buddha of my own mind, with his unconditional great compassion and his great sympathy of one essence with all beings, is in himself inconceivable. Moreover, the causal mind — which is Buddha from the first — with its deep faith and earnest vow and its single-minded, devoted recitation of the name, is also inconceivable. If within thought after thought one can keep removing the various defilements and perfectly reveal the fundamental emptiness of their nature, one will suddenly join the source and go straight to the ocean of the fruit. Therefore, no pure condition surpasses this.

[Dependent arising] Here it means arising from the convergence of many conditions — that is, born of the conjunction of various conditions. [Naturally] by nature. [Causal ground] The whole process from the first stirring of the mind to study the Buddha’s way while still an ordinary person, up until the attainment of perfect Buddhahood, is called the “causal ground.” [Resultant ground] Spoken of in contrast to the “causal ground”: the supreme stage of perfect, wonderful enlightenment attained through cultivation on the causal ground. [One and the same] “One” means equal and non-dual; “same” means ever unchanging. [Inconceivable] that which cannot be fathomed by thought or expressed in words.
[But at the time of reciting, you should let go of all conditions and hold up the single thought alone. As if rescuing your head from burning
(burn)

, as if mourning your parents, as a hen broods her eggs, as a dragon guards its pearl. Look for no small results, seek no quick attainment, but only recite with a single mind, ever and always thus — this is called the supreme, profound, and wondrous gate of Chan. In this way the body of the sense-organs and the world secretly follow the mind,
transformed thought by thought

. This is by no means something an ordinary mind and fleshly eye can know or see. When at last one’s recompense is ended and one’s life is exhausted, Amitābha and the host of sages suddenly appear before one, or there appear wondrous fragrance, celestial music, and various auspicious signs, and only then do people say the pure karma is accomplished. But is the pure karma accomplished only at this moment?]

When reciting the Buddha’s name, you should let go of all conditions and hold up the single thought (the thought of Buddha-recitation) alone. As if rescuing your head from burning, as if mourning your parents, as a hen broods her eggs, as a dragon guards its pearl; look for no small results, seek no quick attainment, but only recite with a single mind, ever and always thus. This is the supreme, profound, and wondrous gate of Chan. In this way the body of the sense-organs and the world secretly follow the mind, being transformed thought by thought. This is not something an ordinary mind and fleshly eye can know or see. When at last one’s recompense is ended and one’s life is exhausted, Amitābha Buddha and the host of sages suddenly appear before one, or there appear wondrous fragrance, celestial music, and various auspicious signs, and only then do people say the pure karma is accomplished. But is the pure karma accomplished only at this moment?

[Root-body] The body composed of the six sense-organs (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). [Various auspicious signs] Master Chewu himself knew the hour of his death ten full months in advance, and at his passing auspicious signs appeared in abundance.
